Issued at 213 AM MST Fri Nov 13 2026

A fairly quiet day is forecast across the Cowboy State for 
Friday. Temperatures to no surprise remain mild with values 10 
to 15 degrees above normal. Highs are expected to reach the 
upper 50s to low 60s east of the Divide and low to mid 50s for 
the west. Aside from mild temperatures, winds will increase in 
the afternoon ahead of an approaching disturbance. These winds 
will be mostly restricted to the Wind Corridor from Rock Springs
to Casper and into Johnson County. Speeds are likely to range 
from 15 to 25 mph with gusts of 30 to 40 mph. A few gusts up to 
45 mph cannot be ruled out.

The aforementioned disturbance is in association with a trough that 
will begin to make its way onshore Friday afternoon. This 
disturbance continues to weaken and become more unorganized which 
will lead to lesser impacts for the area. Showers begin to move into 
western WY Saturday morning with much of the moisture staying across 
the higher elevations. That being said, showers will be 
possible for the lower elevations of western WY throughout the 
day. Temperatures should be cold enough to support snow showers 
during the morning before warming temperatures transition any 
low elevation precipitation into rain. Some showers may be 
possible across southern WY as well, but similar to other low 
elevation locations, amounts will be minimal. East of the Divide
will be quite similar to what has occurred over the past week 
or so. Mild temperatures and mostly dry conditions prevail as 
southwesterly flow will be unfavorable for showers. Due to the 
unorganized nature of the system much of the precipitation will 
end by Sunday. Overall, a coating to maybe an inch of snow is 
possible across the higher elevations of western WY. A very wet 
coating of snow cannot be ruled out for some low elevation 
locations Saturday morning, but the warm temperatures should 
quickly melt any accumulation by the afternoon. Per usual, 
locations east of the Divide will remain dry with mild 
temperatures. Breezy winds will be possible across the same 
locations as Friday.

The remainder of the weekend sees cooler but still above normal 
temperatures with mostly dry conditions. Above normal temperatures 
and dry conditions persist into the start of next week as ridging 
builds back in over the Intermountain West. Another disturbance
is lurking around the corner for the middle of the week. Models
show a trough digging across the western CONUS Monday before 
moving into the Great Basin by Tuesday. This disturbance makes 
its way over the area Tuesday into Wednesday and then quickly 
ejects into the Northern High Plains. The timing of this may be 
a little quick with models possibly slowing the trajectory by 12
to 24 hours as we get closer. At this time, the main things to 
watch will be the track and how well this system can organize. 
Models currently show it remaining mostly unorganized until it 
begins to leave the area where a more defined low begins to 
develop, but by then it will be to the northeast of the area. 
If things stand, the greatest impacts look to be focused across 
western and northwestern WY. These locations would have the most
favorable dynamics to see steady precipitation. As for other 
locations, there does look to be the possibility for some 
widespread precipitation but it would likely be on the lighter 
side. Temperatures may hinder any daytime snowfall mainly for 
locations east of the Divide. Overall, chances for accumulating 
snowfall will be the best across the higher and even lower 
elevations of western WY. Probabilistic guidance is currently 
showing a 30-50% chance for an inch or more of accumulating snow
for the western valleys such as Star Valley and Jackson Hole. 
The higher elevation mountains of western WY have a 30-60% of 3 
or more inches of snow. Other locations see much lower chances 
for any accumulating snowfall due to less favorable dynamics and
warmer temperatures. However, things are not set in stone and 
could possibly change as we head through the weekend. It 
definitely bears monitoring.

Colder more seasonable temperatures look to follow in behind this 
system as it moves out of the region for the second half of the 
week. Longer range models show another disturbance quickly move in 
for the end of the work week into the weekend. As mentioned in 
yesterday's discussion, this system is looking more potent. 
There looks to be greater potential for widespread precipitation
possibly in the form of snow for mostly all elevations. Not to 
be a pessimist, especially for those east of the Divide, but 
with how things have gone the past winter, its best not to get 
overly excited for 200+ hour model depictions. So stay tuned as 
we wait and see what kind of trends may develop over the next 
few days.
